title: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima (1945)
hook: a Jesuit with medical training cares for the wounded after the atomic bomb
carry: he turned the house into a hospital

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salvadoran Jesuits, with Elba and Celina Ramos. Your line was killed for teaching. Which teacher did you thank? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven, the last day of this week.

A Spanish priest is in his room in a Jesuit house on the hills outside Hiroshima, where he trains young men who want to become Jesuits. Before he joined the order, he had studied medicine. He had not practiced as a doctor in years. Then a blinding flash, a roar, and the windows blow in. When he and the others climb the hill and look toward the city, it is burning. Before long, the wounded begin walking out of the smoke and up the road toward them. His name is Pedro Arrupe, and today we watch what he does with a damaged house and some half-forgotten training.
screen: `A JESUIT HOUSE ON THE HILLS.` → `A FLASH, THE WINDOWS BLOW IN.` → `THE WOUNDED WALK UP THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. In his own later account, the house was cracked and battered but still standing. So he and the young Jesuits turned the house into a hospital. The chapel, the rooms, the halls filled with people lying on mats. There was almost no medicine. He writes about doing what little he could with what was on hand, cleaning burns, trying to understand injuries no medical school had ever taught him. The young men became nurses overnight. They went out into the ruins looking for survivors, and they fed people from whatever food they could find. Arrupe did not claim to have been a hero. What he describes is mostly helplessness, and staying anyway. Notice how the whole week gathers here. God in all things, even in a city in flames. Contemplatives in action: a house of prayer that became, without a vote, a house of nursing. Cura personalis, one burned person at a time. The magis, which in that moment simply meant: open the door wider. And yesterday's lesson about teaching that costs something; here it's care that costs something. Jesus, in Matthew's Gospel, names the people he will recognize at the end, and among them, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me." Arrupe later led the whole Society of Jesus. But the story people still tell is this house on the hill, and a man doing the next small thing because he was the one who was there.
screen: `THE HOUSE CRACKED, STILL STANDING.` · `NOVICES BECAME NURSES OVERNIGHT.` · `THE WHOLE WEEK, IN ONE HOUSE.` · `NOT A HERO: STAYING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the victims of war. Settle, and breathe. Picture the road up the hill, and the people walking up it out of the smoke. Then think of one place at war right now, and the people there whose names you'll never know: children, the old, the wounded, and those caring for them with almost nothing. Don't picture the worst. Give them your breathing, one breath at a time. If you pray, you can pray for them and for peace. If you don't, let them stay in your thoughts until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. A Jesuit with old medical training who turned a damaged house of prayer into a hospital for the wounded. Today's word, and the end of this week.
Your line: he turned the house into a hospital. Today, look for one small way to open your own door wider: a seat, a meal, an hour, for someone who needs it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the victims of war and for peace at Mass and in private prayer, and Arrupe's account of caring for the wounded at Hiroshima is often retold in Jesuit schools and retreats.
